notes: Model and effort configuration journeys. What a picker renders is a panel and lives with the panels; these assert the effects -- what becomes active, what the request carries, what a refusal says. The decisive assertion for a switch is not the status line but the request: a turn scripted to answer only when the wire carries the chosen model id or effort, paired with one that answers otherwise, so a change that never reached the wire renders a named string instead of passing. An effort ladder is offered only for a model whose request-fields schema declares an effort enum, which is why the ladder is refused on the entries without one and can be shown to follow the model rather than the session. Its levels are named unlike a real ladder's because a journey asserts them as bare screen text and the obvious names are substrings of the launch tips this lane draws at random. Both commands take a level or model as an argument as well as offering a picker, and both can save the current choice as a default; the save is confirmed but not read back, because nothing in a running session reflects the persisted value. Switches that are not themselves under test are made by id rather than by arrow, so a journey cannot fail on where a picker put its cursor.

scenarios.name: Switching models is reflected in the status line and in what the model receives
scenarios.description: A different model chosen from the picker, then a prompt -- asserts the picker closes, the status line names the new model, and the request carries the chosen model id rather than the previous one
scenarios.observe: A switch that only repaints the status line is indistinguishable from one that took effect, so the load-bearing assertion is the answering turn: it fires only when the request carries both this prompt and the chosen model id, and the paired turn answers the same prompt on any other model, which turns a switch that never reached the wire into a named string rather than a passing run. Both are sticky and both name the prompt, so a background call can neither consume the positive nor be answered by the negative. The confirmation is waited on without its model name, leaving the name a predicate the status line has to satisfy. Choosing the second row rather than the first is what makes this a switch at all -- selecting the active model would confirm and change nothing.

scenarios.name: Switching to a model that does not exist is refused and the active one is kept
scenarios.description: A model id absent from the registry passed to the switch command -- asserts the refusal names the id it could not find and the model it kept, and that the status line still shows the model that was already active
verify: screen.contains:The model 'ghost-model-zzz' is not available. Continuing with Mock KRS Model.
scenarios.observe: A rejected switch has two jobs a bare error does not do: say which id failed, and say what is running now -- without the second a user cannot tell whether they were left on their old model or on nothing. Both are asserted from the one message, and the status-line needle is the independent half: it proves the previously active model is still the one in force rather than merely being named in an alert. The absent success string is what separates a refusal from a switch that reported both.

scenarios.name: Saving the default model targets the model that is active, not the registry default
scenarios.description: The save-as-default command issued after switching models -- asserts the confirmation names the model that was made active rather than the one the registry defaults to
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
verify: screen.contains:Saved Mock KRS Effort Model as default model
scenarios.observe: The switch beforehand is what makes this assertable: with the registry's own default still active, a command that saved the wrong model would produce the same message as one that saved the right one. The write is then proven, not merely confirmed: a fresh session reads the persisted default back on creation and adopts it, so the status line of the new session carries 'Mock KRS Effort Model' rather than the fixture's own default of 'Mock KRS Model'. A confirmation shown without the file being written would leave the new session on the fixture default and fail the status-line needle. The paired negative covers the reported-failure path.

scenarios.name: The chosen effort level is in the request the model receives
scenarios.description: A non-default effort level chosen from the picker, then a prompt -- asserts the choice is confirmed, shown in the status line, and present in the request body under the path the registry's schema declared
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
scenarios.observe: An effort level a user selects is worth nothing if it does not reach the model, and no panel can show whether it did. The answering turn is matched on the request body carrying the effort at the path the registry's schema declared, so it can only fire once the selection has been serialized into the request; the paired turn answers the same prompt without it, which turns a level that stopped at the status line into a named string. Both are sticky and both name the prompt, so a background call can neither consume the positive nor be answered by the negative. The confirmation is waited on without its level, leaving the level a predicate the status line has to satisfy.

scenarios.name: An effort level given as an argument applies without opening the picker
scenarios.description: A valid effort level passed directly to the effort command -- asserts it is confirmed and reaches the status line, and that no picker was opened on the way
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
scenarios.observe: The argument form is a separate code path from the picker and is the one a user scripts or repeats, so it is worth its own journey. The confirmation is waited on without its level, leaving the level a predicate the status line has to satisfy; the absent picker header is what proves the argument was applied directly rather than falling back to a menu. The absent refusal covers the path where the level is accepted by the command but never adopted, which reports the level as unavailable rather than failing outright.

scenarios.name: An effort level the model does not advertise is refused and the current level stands
scenarios.description: A level absent from the advertised ladder passed to the effort command -- asserts the refusal names the level and that the level already in force is unchanged
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
scenarios.observe: The runtime accepts a level it does not advertise and silently leaves the effort unchanged, so the client has to notice and say so -- this pins that it does, by name. The status-line needle is the independent half and the more important one: it proves the level in force is still the advertised default rather than the rejected string, which is what a user would otherwise have no way to check. The absent success string separates a refusal from a switch that reported both.

scenarios.name: Saving the default effort names both the level and the model it applies to
scenarios.description: The save-as-default effort command issued after choosing a level -- asserts the confirmation names the chosen level and the model it was saved for
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
verify: screen.contains:Set exhaustive as default effort for Mock KRS Effort Model
scenarios.observe: An effort default is stored per model, so a confirmation that named only the level would leave a user unable to tell which model it was stored against. Both halves are asserted from the one message, and the chosen level is not the advertised default, so a command that saved whatever was already in force would name the wrong one. Unlike the default-model journey, the write is not proven here: a new session and a switch away and back both re-adopt the schema's own default rather than the saved level in this lane, so nothing in-session reflects the persisted effort. The assertion is therefore the confirmation only; the persisted-effort round trip has no observable surface a journey can reach from here.

scenarios.name: Switching to a model without effort levels takes the ladder away again
scenarios.description: An effort-capable model made active, its ladder opened, then a model advertising none made active -- asserts the ladder is gone rather than left over from the previous model
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Plain Model
scenarios.observe: A ladder that appeared for one model and was still offered after switching to a model that advertises none would let a user select a level the request cannot carry, so what this pins is the withdrawal. The run reaches the ladder first -- the wait for the picker is what makes this a withdrawal rather than a ladder that never appeared -- then switches and waits for the refusal. The status-line needle is the assertion: the model name followed straight by the context gauge means no level sits between them, and the paired negative names the level that was in force on the previous model, so a chip left behind fails rather than passing quietly.

scenarios.name: Effort commands on a model that has none are refused with the way forward
scenarios.description: The effort picker and the save-as-default command both issued while a model without effort levels is active -- asserts each refusal names the limitation, names the model it applies to, and tells the user what would let them proceed
steps: waitForText:Effort is not available on the current model. Select a model that supports effort levels.
waitForText:No effort level is currently set.
verify: screen.contains:Effort may not be available on Mock KRS Model.
scenarios.observe: A command that cannot apply is only well behaved if it says why and what to do instead, so the picker refusal is waited on in full including the remedy -- the half a user acts on, and the half a refusal is likeliest to drop. The save-as-default command is a separate code path that produces its own single-sentence refusal; the gate takes its first clause and the predicate its remainder, so what the predicate independently adds over the gate is the model-name interpolation -- naming the active model is what tells a user the limitation belongs to their model rather than to the command. The two success strings are asserted absent because neither command may quietly appear to have worked, and the absent picker header proves the first refusal replaced the ladder rather than opening an empty one. Only the save-default refusal is asserted from the screen: these are transient alerts, and it has replaced the picker refusal by the time the predicates run.
